name: Demand
kicker: Economics concept · How much buyers want at each possible price
briefing: Demand is the economic idea that explains why a brand-new video game costs more on release day than it does a year later: it is simply how much of something people are willing and able to buy at each possible price. Economists graph it as a downward-sloping curve, since people usually want more of something when it gets cheaper and less when it gets pricier. Where that curve crosses the supply curve sets a market’s price.

tossups.p: Economists distinguish this concept’s “Marshallian” and “Hicksian” mathematical forms, which the Slutsky equation relates to each other. One famous exception to this concept’s usual law is named for the Scottish economist Robert Giffen, whose namesake goods become more wanted as their price rises.
tossups.r: A second exception, named for Thorstein Veblen, covers luxury goods that become more desirable as they get pricier. For 10 points, name this economic concept, usually graphed as a downward-sloping curve and often paired with supply.

tossups.p: This concept’s “price elasticity” was analyzed in a landmark 1890 textbook by economist Alfred Marshall. Economists study this concept “ceteris paribus [“SEH-teh-ris PAH-ree-bus”],” meaning they hold every other factor constant except price.
tossups.r: For “normal goods,” this quantity rises as a buyer’s income rises, while for “inferior goods” it falls. For 10 points, name this economic concept, the amount of a good that consumers want to buy, which is often graphed against supply.

tossups.p: In the labor market, economists say that businesses, rather than workers, are the side that wants to “buy,” since employers are the ones seeking workers. In business, a chain version of this concept, built from marketing, sales, and service, mirrors the more familiar supply chain.
tossups.r: Giffen goods and Veblen goods are both famous exceptions to this concept’s usual law. For 10 points, name this economic concept, graphed as a curve that typically slopes downward as price rises.

tossups.p: The Hicksian version of this concept is defined by minimizing how much a consumer spends while holding their satisfaction, or “utility,” fixed. Robert Giffen gave his name to a category of goods that break this concept’s usual law by becoming more wanted as they get pricier.
tossups.r: This concept is sometimes described as a measure of consumers’ “willingness to pay” for a good. For 10 points, name this economic concept, usually drawn as a downward-sloping curve and set against supply.

tossups.p: Thorstein Veblen’s name is given to a type of good, often a luxury item, that breaks this concept’s usual law by becoming more desirable as its price rises. Alfred Marshall’s 1890 textbook studied how strongly this quantity reacts to changes in price, a property called its elasticity.
tossups.r: Economists separate this concept itself from one single point on its own curve, tied to one exact price. For 10 points, name this economic concept, usually graphed as sloping downward against price.

tossups.p: This concept’s usual law holds that, all else equal, a lower price usually means people want to buy more of something. The income effect describes how this quantity changes as a buyer’s real income rises or falls.

tossups.r: This concept is usually graphed as a downward-sloping curve and set against its opposite, supply, to find a market’s equilibrium price. For 10 points, name this economic concept, the quantity of a good that buyers want.

trap.title: Demand, or quantity demanded?
trap.body: “Demand” is the whole relationship between price and quantity, shown as an entire curve. “Quantity demanded” is just one specific amount at one specific price, a single point sitting on that curve. Real answer lines sometimes want one term and not the other, and a question about a price change moving along the curve usually means “quantity demanded” changed, not “demand” itself.
trap.fix: If the clue describes the whole curve shifting (because of income, tastes, or the price of other goods), say “demand.” If it describes one point at one price, “quantity demanded” is the sharper answer — but both are accepted here.
